newsitem.title: USA: Gore offers emergency aid to storm-ravaged West.
newsitem.headline: Gore offers emergency aid to storm-ravaged West.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore flew Friday to this small California town where hundreds fought desperately to hold back floods and praised them as "the real heroes" in the West's New Year storms.

Earlier, during a visit to storm-battered Seattle, Gore said the federal government would provide $42 million in emergency funds to help rebuild damaged roads in five states hit by storms and floods in the last two weeks.

Inspecting two earth walls built quickly to keep out floods from the town of Meridian, 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento, Gore said the effort was "one of the finest examples of neighbours helping neighbours I've seen."
"The people who built the levees around this town so quickly are the real heroes," Gore said.

About 200 people, including volunteers and state prison inmates, worked around the clock to build the wall when a levee on a swollen river broke early this week, threatening to deluge Meridian, a town of 400 people. When water began seeping through the first wall, they built a second one, which has so far succeeded in keeping out the water.

Gore, wearing a blue denim shirt and jeans, helped throw a few sandbags on the makeshift levee. John Bartlett, an official helping to supervise the operation, told Gore: "I think we could have used you a couple of days ago."

President Clinton has declared federal disaster areas in parts of California, Idaho and Nevada, and outgoing Gov. Mike Lowry is preparing a formal request of aid for Washington, where 35 of 39 counties were declared state emergency areas. Heavy flooding also hit Oregon.

On Friday, California Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency due to floods in two more counties, bringing the total to 44 of the state's 58 counties. Mayor Willie Brown also declared a local state of emergency in San Francisco, citing storm damage to property of nearly $3.5 million.
In California alone, damage estimates have passed $1.5 billion. The California Office of Emergency Services said 2,676 homes were destroyed and 8,705 suffered minor damage.

On Friday, the California Department of Food and Agriculture estimated initial flood damage to agriculture at nearly $155 million, including $68 million in damage to farm buildings and infrastructure, $51 million in crop losses and $22 million in livestock and milk production losses.

In California, Gore also announced that the state would receive $9 million for the costs of fighting the flood and the U.S. Department of Labour said it would provide up to $25 million to create temporary jobs in flood cleanup.
Most California rivers are now receding although some areas remain submerged. Two levees broke in San Joaquin County in central California Friday, flooding new areas and threatening homes.

Gore, accompanied by other officials, flew to Meridian by helicopter for a one-hour visit. "Flying over the flood was an incredible experience. Seeing it on TV does not capture the extent of this tragedy," said Gore, who was also scheduled to visit flood-hit Idaho.
At a town hall-style meeting in a fire station north of Seattle earlier, Gore said the emergency relief he announced was "only the beginning" of the federal response to the storms.

"We're going to be your partners in responding to this disaster every step of the way," he told officials in Shoreline, a newly incorporated city where he saw a road split by a yawning sinkhole 150 feet (50 metres) wide.
